correctness.rationale: For a unit-edge tree with m edges, normalized whole-tree arclength gives density [2m(1-r)_+ +2 Σ_{k≥0} N_k g(r-k)]/m² with g triangular on [0,2]. End-point minimum edge distance k gives the two independent offsets; f(0+)=2/m determines m, and triangular integer translates are linearly independent, so law equality iff edge-separation histogram agrees. Both displayed eight-edge trees independently have histogram (10,10,6,2), different degree multisets/leaf counts, and the displayed four-interval piecewise density. Independent enumeration of all 1,1,2,3,6,11,23 nonisomorphic trees with n=2..8 (NetworkX independent unlabeled generator; no histogram collisions) and all 47 nonisomorphic 9-vertex trees (45 distinct histogram classes) verifies sharp first collision. The source Prüfer script exhausts all 8^6 labeled trees through n8, furnishing separate finite certificate.

originality.rationale: The full two-point metric-measure inverse problem and counterexamples are old (Mémoli–Needham); Hosoya edge/vertex polynomial equivalence is explicitly known from Tratnik–Žigert Pleteršek Theorem 3.2. The claimed contribution is only the sharp smallest nine-unit-vertex threshold, pair with different leaf count and explicit continuous density. A prior enumerated same-Hosoya table might implicitly determine minimality; unavailable full Mémoli text remains a genuine specific priority risk, although no decisively covering statement was observed.

Unit edges and uniform whole-tree arclength are essential; arbitrary edge lengths may yield smaller examples.

value.rationale: This is a natural complete finite cutoff for the intrinsic metric-tree distance inverse problem: an apparently rich continuous distance law first fails at exactly nine vertices and cannot even reconstruct leaf count. Exhaustive small-tree classification is meaningful, not an arbitrary finite invariant, and the precise density gives a reusable reconstruction benchmark.
